The answer for Colordle #1515 on May 18, 2026, is Tangerine. The hex code is #FF9300. This color is a pure, high-saturation orange with no blue mixed in. If you landed on it, great. What kind of color this is

Tangerine lives firmly in the orange hue family. Looking at the hex code #FF9300, you see maximum red (FF), a significant amount of green (93), and zero blue (00). That lack of blue is the tell. It keeps the color from muddying into brown or cooling down into a terracotta. It is bright, citrusy, and aggressive.

Coming off a streak of cool colors like Cobalt yesterday and Blue Purple the day before, this feels like a deliberate reset. The game swung from the deepest cool blues to a blazing warm orange. We saw White and Grass earlier in the week, so the palette has been bouncing around. Tangerine doesn't try to be subtle. It sits right in the middle of the orange range, avoiding the yellow lean of Amber or the red lean of Vermilion. If your last guess was a muted peach, you were too soft. This color demands full saturation.

How to narrow your guesses toward it

When the hue bar points to orange, the trap is assuming all oranges look the same. They don't. The difference between Tangerine and, say, Coral, is the red-to-green ratio. In #FF9300, the green value (93) is just high enough to keep it orange but low enough to avoid yellow. If you guessed a yellow-orange and the game told you "warmer," you needed more red. If it said "cooler," you needed less red or more yellow.

Start with a pure orange anchor. If you don't have one memorized, try standard web oranges. Watch the saturation feedback closely. Tangerine is fully saturated. If the game indicates your guess is too dull, increase the intensity. Many players waste turns shifting hue when they should be adjusting saturation. For a breakdown of how saturation affects scoring, see our Colordle strategy guide. Also, ensure your device calibration isn't lying to you; some screens push oranges toward red. Trust the hex values if the visual cue feels off.

Where players usually go wrong

The biggest mistake with Tangerine is confusing it with golden or amber tones. Players see "orange" and immediately think of autumn leaves or pumpkins, which often have brownish undertones. Tangerine #FF9300 has none of that earthiness. It is synthetic and bright. Another common error is overcorrecting for the previous day's Cobalt. After seeing such a deep, dark blue, some players subconsciously avoid high-intensity colors, guessing softer apricots instead. Don't second-guess the intensity.

Also, avoid the red-orange trap. While Tangerine is warm, it is not close to red. If your guess was closer to #FF4500 (OrangeRed), you were too far left on the spectrum. The game rewards precision here. You need to find that sweet spot where red and green mix without blue dragging it down or red dominating it. If you are struggling to distinguish these shades, our color difference explainer breaks down how the algorithm calculates distance between these similar hues.

How the score logic actually helps

Colordle's scoring isn't just about right or wrong; the numerical score tells you exactly how far off you are in 3D color space. A score in the 20s means you are in the right neighborhood but missed the mark on saturation or lightness. A score in the 60s or 70s means you are in the wrong hue family entirely. With Tangerine, if you guessed a yellow and got a high score, the system is telling you that you are far from the zero-blue zone of true orange.

Use the score to triangulate. If you guess a light peach and get a moderate score, then guess a dark brown and get a terrible score, you know the answer is bright. The logic holds up if you treat the score as a distance metric, not a grade. It measures Euclidean distance in RGB space. For Tangerine, the lack of blue makes the Z-axis easy to lock down. Once you know Blue is 0, you only have to balance Red and Green. This reduces the problem from 3D to 2D, making it much easier to solve in fewer turns. If you're one guess away and can't figure out why your (255, 150, 70) looks wrong, drop the red by about 40 points.

How to read the visual hints

Colorfle's feedback system gives you three distance indicators per guess, but most players over-weight the directional arrows and under-weight the magnitude of the numbers. Here's what actually matters for May 26:

  • Red channel (217): High but not extreme. If your first guess was 240+ red and got "close," the answer is slightly lower than you thought, not higher.
  • Green channel (153): This is the sneaky one. The green is more than half of the red value, which creates the amber warmth. Guesses with green below 120 will read too red or too orange-brown.
  • Blue channel (71): The blue is doing heavy lifting despite being the lowest value. Remove it entirely and you get a harsh orange. That 71 blue is what mutes and sophisticates the color.

I usually start with a neutral gray guess — #808080 — to establish midline baselines. Today that strategy paid off fast because the answer is above midline in red and green but below in blue. One player in my Discord mentioned they guessed pure blue (#0000FF) second, which sounds wasteful but actually isolated the blue channel's relative weakness quickly. Not my approach, but valid.

Last week's colors were dominated by extreme values — one answer was essentially pure magenta, another was near-black with a single channel spike. Today's spread across all three channels rewards players who methodically bracket rather than chase single-channel hunches.

Common wrong approaches

I tried subtractive logic on my second guess today. Dropped blue to 20, bumped red and green. The color I got was a muddy rust that looked nothing like the target. That's because Colorfle simulates light addition, not pigment blending. In paint, adding blue to orange dulls toward neutral. In RGB, adding blue shifts the hue toward... still orange, but a lighter, chalkier orange because you're raising the overall luminance of the darker channel.

Another trap: treating "close" feedback as directional. If the game says your green is close, players often nudge it by 10-15 points. Today the green sits at 153. If you guessed 140 and got "close," the jump to 153 is bigger than the feedback granularity suggests. I see people inching toward answers when they should be leaping. Don't trust your monitor if you're on a cheap laptop. I dual-screen between a calibrated Dell and a baseline MacBook Air, and today's color looks distinctly more yellow on the MacBook. The RGB values are objective; your perception isn't. When in doubt, trust the numbers over your eyes.

Why does the answer look brown on my phone but orange on my desktop?

Display color temperature and gamut vary wildly between OLED phones and budget LCD monitors. The RGB values are fixed, but your brain interprets the surrounding white point differently. I see this most with mid-tone ambers and desaturated magentas. Today's answer is particularly susceptible because none of the channels are extreme — there's no 255 or 0 anchoring the color to a clear hue category.

The solver tool is honestly faster than either manual method once you've played enough to read its suggestions.

Think about shining three colored flashlights at a wall. More light is always brighter, never darker. When you add blue to orange light, you're not making mud — you're adding luminance in a third channel that shifts the mixed color toward white. Today's answer only works as a color because that blue channel is present but restrained. If you catch yourself thinking "blue cancels orange," stop. It doesn't.

Because "close" in Colorfle covers a range. Your guess was within about 15 points on each channel, but the cumulative error put you in a perceptually different zone — too saturated, slightly too red. The solver would flag that your Euclidean distance was still significant. I had a similar guess today; the channel-by-channel feedback felt encouraging but the visual mismatch was obvious. That's the game telling you to adjust all three channels simultaneously, not just hunt the one "far" signal.

I personally guessed "debt" at #3, felt clever, then spun for ten minutes. That's the trap. Contexto punishes you for finding a strong semantic neighbor and assuming you're close in the ranking. You're not. "Debt" and "credit" are conceptually joined at the hip, but the model weights them differently depending on training context. I see this pattern about twice a week.

Need a reset? Our Contexto archive has every answer back to January 2024, sorted by date. Useful for spotting whether the puzzle leans abstract or concrete on any given day.

What the clues are telling you

Today's top hint words from the Contexto system, if you're playing the unlimited version or seeing partial reveals:

  • #2 TRUST — The strongest signal. If you hit this, you're one conceptual hop away.
  • #5 LOAN — Keeps you in the financial lane, which is correct but narrow.
  • #11 BELIEF — This is where players derail. The algorithm is picking up "credit" as in "give credit," not just Visa and Mastercard.
  • #23 CARD — Too specific. "Credit card" is a phrase, but the model doesn't treat compounds kindly.

The #11 ranking for "belief" is the tell. I watched three people in a Discord thread ignore it because they were tunnel-visioned on banking. Contexto doesn't care about your category boxes. The vector for "credit" pulls from academic citations, movie credits, and personal reputation as much as it does from APR and FICO scores.

If your guesses are landing in the #40-#80 range and feeling "close but wrong," try abstracting. Ask what connects your guesses rather than what distinguishes them. That's usually the bridge.

When to guess vs when to think

There's a rhythm to Contexto that took me months to trust. Early guesses should be broad category probes. Middle game is where you map the semantic field. Late game is when you start playing word-association chicken with the algorithm.

Today, if you had "bank" at #7 and "money" at #12, the temptation is to drill down: "savings," "checking," "account." That's guessing. The better move is to lateral. What else sits near "bank" and "money" but isn't them? "Credit" is the obvious answer in hindsight, but "trust," "faith," and "reputation" all signal the same vector neighborhood.

I use a simple rule now: if three guesses in a row don't break into the top 5, I switch domains entirely. From finance to philosophy, or from objects to actions. The model's top clusters are usually narrower than your intuition suggests. Today's puzzle is a perfect case study—the answer sits at the intersection of two domains most players treat as separate.

Our Contexto solver tool can help you visualize these clusters if you're playing the unlimited version and want to train your intuition. It doesn't give answers; it maps similarity spaces. I've found it useful for understanding why "debt" ranks closer than "visa" even though the latter is physically on a credit card.

Questions players keep asking

Why does Contexto rank "credit" higher than "credibility" when they share a root?

The model doesn't parse morphology the way humans do. "Credit" as a noun has more training overlap with financial and social trust contexts. "Credibility" is more academic and rhetorical. The vectors diverge more than you'd expect. I've seen "credible" rank at #31 on a similar puzzle while "credit" sat at #1.

How does Contexto handle words with multiple meanings?

Poorly, from a human perspective. Brilliantly, from a distributional semantics perspective. "Credit" means both "academic unit" and "financial trust." The model averages these senses into a single vector. Your job is to guess the averaged point, not any individual meaning. That's why words like "trust" and "faith" rank high—they're also polysemous in overlapping ways.

Is there a faster way to solve when I'm stuck in the #20-#50 range?

Yes. Stop guessing synonyms and start guessing antonyms or functional equivalents. If "debt" is at #3 and you're stuck, try what debt enables or contrasts with. "Purchase," "spend," "borrow." Sometimes the model's path to your target runs through action verbs, not nouns. I cleared a #32 rut on Tuesday by switching from nouns to verbs entirely.

Why did my answer work yesterday but rank terribly today?

Because the target word changed. The model is static; the puzzle is daily. Your "instinct" for what Contexto likes is actually pattern-matching against past target distributions. Some days the answer is concrete ("hammer," #847 from March). Some days it's abstract like today. The archive helps you calibrate. I review it weekly to see if the editors are clustering around themes.

Does playing more Contexto actually improve your score?

Marginally, and then it plateaus. What improves is your tolerance for semantic noise. You stop expecting clean categories. You start seeing "close" as a directional hint, not a frustration. I'm not faster than I was at 200 puzzles, but I quit fewer games in anger. That counts for something.

Count your characters. Multiplication in an eight-slot Nerdle almost always needs a single-digit times double-digit to stay within bounds, like 7*8=56 or 6*9=54. Four boards, nine guesses, and that familiar panic when you realize your third guess only cleared one letter on the bottom-left grid. I've been here since Quordle launched in early 2022, and the May 26 puzzle is a solid midweek test—nothing brutal, but it'll punish lazy starting words.

Today's Quordle at a glance

May 26's classic mode hands you a mix: two answers lean on common consonant clusters, one has a repeated vowel pattern that'll mess with your rhythm, and the fourth is sneakily short on unique letters. If you're staring at four yellows and no greens after guess two, you're not alone. I burned my fourth guess chasing a phantom 'R' on the top-right board because I refused to believe the word didn't have one.

The Quordle Solver tool flagged my mistake immediately—turns out I'd locked into a word that fit three boards perfectly and ignored the fourth. Classic Quordle tunnel vision. For today's puzzle, starting with a word like "SLATE" or "CRANE" gives you decent coverage, but don't sleep on second-guess words that test less common letters. "MOUND" or "GIPSY" can break open a board that's going cold.

What the clues are telling you

When a letter shows yellow on all four boards, you've got a decision: is it in the same position on multiple grids, or scattered? Today, that happened to me with 'E'—yellow everywhere, green nowhere. I wasted a guess parking it in slot three when two boards wanted it in slot five. The Wordle archive has trained me to trust frequency, but Quordle punishes that instinct. You need positional flexibility.

Green tiles are your anchors, obviously, but pay attention to what's not showing up. A board with zero yellows after three guesses isn't necessarily stubborn—it's probably built from letters you've already eliminated elsewhere. I keep a mental (okay, sometimes written) list of dead letters per board, not just globally. On May 26's puzzle, that saved me: 'V' was dead on three boards but essential on the fourth, where I almost talked myself out of it.

For chill mode players, this is less urgent—you've got guesses to burn. But in extreme mode, where every guess must be a valid answer word, today's repeated vowel board is a trap. You can't just throw "AAHED" at it and hope; your guesses have to be real words that fit constraints across all boards. I use the daily answer page to backcheck my logic after solving, which helps calibrate for tomorrow.

When to guess vs when to think

There's a moment in every Quordle solve where one board looks almost done and the others are chaos. The mistake is always the same: you slam in the word that fits the clean board and get two letters wrong on the messy ones. Today, I had _IGHT on the bottom board and "FIGHT" felt obvious. It was right, but guessing it cost me a letter-check I needed elsewhere. Should have played "MIGHT" first to test 'M' on another board.

Here's my rule now: if a word solves one board but gives zero new info on the others, pause. Can you find a guess that advances two boards? Even advancing one messy board by one letter beats a quick solve on a solved board. The exception is sequence mode, where boards unlock one by one—totally different calculus. In sequence, May 26's puzzle flows smoother if you treat each unlocked board as a fresh Wordle with carryover eliminated letters. The sequence mode guide breaks that down better than I can in a paragraph.

Rescue mode today? Brutal if you didn't start strong. You're fixing broken guesses, and the fixed letters don't always cooperate. I saw someone on Reddit mention they treat rescue like a cryptic crossword—work backwards from constraints. Not wrong.

Questions players keep asking

Why does Quordle sometimes reject valid words?

It doesn't, but your brain does. You've probably played Wordle mode so long that you forget Quordle's answer list is broader. "SOARE" works. "XYLAN" works. If it's a real English word and the game says no, double-check your spelling—I've typed "RECIEVE" more times than I care to admit. The game uses standard dictionaries, no weird proper nouns.

How do I not run out of guesses in extreme mode?

Build a stable of 15-20 strong starting words that cover letter frequency, but more importantly, practice pivoting. Extreme mode doesn't let you guess "SOARE" then "DOILY" just to test letters—every guess must be a possible answer. So your first guess needs to be a real word, your second needs to be a real word that fits what you know, and so on. I keep a personal list of "bridging" words that are boring but flexible: "STARE," "POINT," "CLIME." Nothing sexy, but they don't paint you into corners.

Does the weekly mode have different difficulty?

Not officially, but the pacing feels different because you're carrying stress across seven days. Miss Monday hard and you're chasing points all week. May 26 is a Wednesday, so mid-week puzzles tend to be calibrated for that sweet spot where you need focus but not a thesaurus. The weekly archive shows difficulty ratings player-submitted, if you want to calibrate your own sense of "hard."

Where can I find past Quordle answers?

The Quordle archive goes back to 2022, though early data is spotty. For tracking your own streak or checking whether "KNOLL" has already been an answer (it has, twice), that's your spot. I use it to avoid starter words that were recent answers—no point opening with "APPLE" if it was last week's solution.

Still stuck? The solver tool handles multi-board logic better than my brain at 6:45 AM. Use it, learn from it, then try tomorrow's puzzle raw. That's the loop.

searchle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Searchle Answer Today: May 26, 2026

The answer to today's Searchle puzzle (May 26, 2026) is solar flare effects on earth. The autocomplete suggestions were dominated by immediate concerns: power grid stability, satellite communication delays, and aurora visibility maps. If you spent the morning refreshing space weather apps like half the internet, this query probably felt obvious. For everyone else, the hints pointed squarely at atmospheric interference rather than the source event itself.

We updated the Searchle archive with today's solution, so you can verify your streak or see where you went off-track. If you're stuck on tomorrow's puzzle, our daily hint tool breaks down the semantic clusters before you waste a guess.

Today's Searchle at a glance

Today's puzzle was less about pop culture and more about the news cycle. The target query, 'solar flare effects on earth,' has been trending since the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration issued a G4 storm watch three days ago. The autocomplete suggestions didn't hide this; they practically screamed it. You saw fragments like 'solar flare effects on earth power grid' and 'solar flare effects on earth humans' dominating the prediction list.

What tripped a lot of players up was the specificity of the noun. Many guessed 'aurora borealis' or 'geomagnetic storm,' which are related but aren't the exact high-volume query Google prioritizes right now. The game algorithm favors the most typed phrase, not necessarily the most scientifically precise term. I made the same mistake on my first attempt, typing 'solar flare damage,' which returned zero matches in the suggestion list. That zero-match result was the real clue—it told me I needed the standard, slightly clunky phrasing that news outlets use.

If you need a quick reset, check the Searchle solver tool to test different phrasing against historical autocomplete data. It saves you from burning guesses on synonyms that look right but don't match the search volume.

What the clues are telling you

The hint system today was generous if you know how to read the room. The first hint mentioned 'atmospheric interference,' which should have immediately ruled out space-only terms like 'coronal mass ejection.' The second hint referenced 'radio blackouts,' a classic symptom of solar activity that directly impacts daily life. These weren't abstract riddles; they were direct references to the headlines running all week.

Searchle often pulls from 'evergreen' topics that suddenly spike due to current events. Space weather is a perfect example. It's always there, but it only becomes a 'Searchle' topic when the sun decides to act up. The clues reflected this urgency. They didn't ask about the physics of the sun; they asked about the consequences here. That distinction is critical. When the hints focus on impact rather than origin, narrow your search to phrases containing 'on earth,' 'impact on,' or 'effects of.'

Don't ignore the length of the suggestions either. The target query was six words long. If your guess was three words, you were likely too broad. The autocomplete engine favors specific, long-tail queries during high-interest events because that's what people are actually typing into the search bar.

When to guess vs when to think

In puzzles like this, speed is dangerous. My instinct was to type 'solar storm' immediately because it's shorter and cleaner. Bad move. In Searchle, 'clean' often means 'wrong' because the general public types verbose, question-based queries. You have to think like a worried homeowner, not an astronomer. A homeowner types 'solar flare effects on earth power outages.' An astronomer types 'geomagnetic induction.' The game wants the homeowner.

Wait for the autocomplete list to populate fully before committing. If you type 'solar flare' and the suggestions immediately drop down with 'effects on earth' as the top prediction, you have your answer. Don't overthink it by trying to find a clever synonym. The game isn't testing your vocabulary; it's testing your ability to mimic the average searcher. If the top suggestion matches your mental model of the news cycle, lock it in.

However, if you see a suggestion that looks slightly off—like 'solar flare effects on skin'—pause. That's a distractor. While scientifically plausible in extreme sci-fi scenarios, it's not the dominant search trend. Stick to the infrastructure and communication angles; that's where the real search volume lives during these events.

Questions players keep asking

Why didn't 'northern lights' work as an answer?

'Northern lights' is a valid phenomenon caused by solar flares, but it wasn't the specific query trending today. Searchle targets the exact phrasing with the highest search volume. While people were searching for auroras, the volume for 'solar flare effects on earth' was significantly higher due to news coverage about power grids and satellites. Always prioritize the phrase that encompasses the broader news narrative, not just the pretty outcome.

How does Searchle choose its daily topics?

The game pulls from real-time and trending Google Autocomplete data. When a major event happens—like a G4 solar storm, a celebrity scandal, or a tech outage—the associated queries spike. The algorithm selects the most distinct, high-volume query related to that event. It's not random; it's a reflection of what the world is curious about right now. You can often predict the topic by checking trending news before you even open the game.

Can I use previous Searchle answers to help me?

Absolutely. Reviewing the past answers archive helps you spot patterns in how the game handles current events versus evergreen trivia. You'll notice that during news spikes, the answers are longer and more descriptive. During quiet periods, they lean toward pop culture or simple facts. Understanding this rhythm helps you calibrate your guesses faster.

What happens if I run out of guesses?

If you exhaust your attempts, the answer is revealed, and your streak resets. There's no penalty other than pride. To avoid this, use the hint system strategically. Don't burn a guess just to test a hunch. Wait until you have at least two confirming data points from the autocomplete suggestions or hints. Patience beats speed in Searchle.

semantle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Semantle Answer Today — May 26, 2026

I burned six guesses on "emotion" and its relatives this morning before I stopped chasing the obvious. That's the trap Semantle sets: the answer feels like it should sit next to your warm words, but it's often one conceptual hop away. Today's word is no exception. If you're seeing greens in the 30s and can't break through, your problem is specificity.

Today's Semantle at a glance

The answer for May 26, 2026 is TINGLE. It's a noun and verb, most commonly describing that light prickling sensation on skin—goosebumps without the bumps, basically. Think of the feeling when someone walks over your grave, or when a song hits just right.

What makes this one tricky: most players' first associations with bodily sensations are broader. "Shiver" scores a respectable 38. "Chill" hits 34. "Thrill" lands at 42, which feels close until you realize it's pulling from a different emotional register. "Tingle" is more physical than emotional, more precise than "feeling." That's the gap.

My own solve path went: SENSE (27) → FEELING (31) → REACTION (22, wrong track) → SENSATION (45) → TINGLE (100). That jump from 45 to 100 is classic Semantle. You're in the right semantic cloud, but you need the exact word the embedding model clustered most tightly.

What the clues are telling you

Today's clue widget shows the 1000th-closest word scoring at 14.2, which is slightly higher than average. That tells you the answer isn't wildly obscure—it's just specific. When the floor is higher, the target word tends to be something everyday players would recognize, not some Word2vec outlier like "ziggurat" or "quiddity."

Here's what my nearest guesses looked like:

  • SHIVER — 38.7
  • PRICKLE — 52.1
  • NUMBNESS — 19.4
  • SENSATION — 45.0
  • TINGLE — 100.0

"Prickle" being closer than "shiver" is the key tell. The model groups by physical sensation type, not just intensity. If you're getting warmth from words describing surface-level skin reactions, stay in that lane. "Goosebumps" itself scores 51.3, which should have been my signal to think about what causes them rather than the phenomenon itself.

The Semantle archive shows this answer falls in a cluster with other May puzzles—last year's May 14th answer was "SHUDDER," and the 28th was "QUIVER." There's something about late spring that pulls somatic vocabulary.

When to guess vs when to think

Semantle rewards a weird rhythm. Burn three guesses fast to map the space, then pause. I see too many players spam synonyms when one or two data points would redirect them.

Today, if you had SHIVER at 38, the move isn't to try CHILL, COLD, FEVER. The model already told you you're in the right neighborhood but wrong house. Think about what shiver and goosebumps share mechanistically. It's not temperature. It's the nervous system's surface-level response.

I keep a solver tool bookmarked for days like this—not to cheat, but to check my intuition after I'm stuck. If I've been chasing a thread for ten guesses and my highest is under 50, something's wrong with my category, not my vocabulary. Today's puzzle is a good example: "emotion" and "tingle" live in different enough vector space that you can waste a dozen guesses bridging them.

Hard mode tip: if you're playing without the clue widget, watch for when your guesses start clustering in a tight score range. That means you're orbiting the target but not closing distance. Pivot to more specific or more basic words, not lateral synonyms.

Questions players keep asking

Why does "feeling" score lower than "sensation"?

Word2vec trains on co-occurrence in text, not dictionary definitions. "Feeling" is massively polysemous—it covers emotions, opinions, physical states, intuitions. The model spreads its vector across all those meanings, diluting any single direction. "Sensation" is more tightly bound to physical experience, so it lands closer to "tingle." This is why broad words often underperform in Semantle even when they feel right.

Is there a pattern to when answers are verbs vs nouns?

Not strictly, but there's a bias toward common nouns in the 30-60 difficulty range. Verbs are trickier because English verbs carry more grammatical contexts. Today's answer works as both, which probably pulled it toward the center of the distribution—neither the easiest nor hardest puzzle this month. The May 12th answer was pure verb, "GLEAM," and played notably harder.

How do I recover from a wrong semantic category?

Look at your highest-scoring guess and ask what specific domain it belongs to. If you guessed "emotion" early and got 31, don't chase more emotions. Ask: what kind of emotion? Physical? Mental? Then test the boundary. Today, that boundary-crossing guess might be "BUTTERFLIES" (29.6), which bridges emotional and physical. From there, you're one step from the somatic cluster.

Does the time of day affect puzzle difficulty?

No, but your cognitive state does. I solve worse at 6am before coffee. The puzzles don't change; my willingness to sit with ambiguity does. Today's word took me longer than it should have because I was rushing. The 2026 archive is full of puzzles I botched on first pass and nailed in two minutes later. There's no prize for speed, so if you're stuck, walk away. The embedding space will still be there.

Today's puzzle in context

I see players in Discord guessing the obvious mascot every time that universe pops up. Don't be that person. The answer today is a side character, not the face of the series.

Which attributes matter most today

How do I avoid wasting guesses on the wrong weight class?

Does the Smashdle Solver work for all game modes?

Classic and hard mode, yes. The daily challenge with rotating restrictions? Only if the filter set matches standard attributes. Check the mode banner before relying on the solver. I've had days where the restricted pool broke my usual workflow.

Why does jump count trip people up so often?

Because it's not intuitive from the fighter's design. Little Mac looks like he jumps once and collapses. He doesn't. Meta Knight looks floaty. He isn't, not in the data. Your eyes lie. The numbers don't. Trust the solver over your visual read.

Where do I find yesterday's answer if I missed it?

The Smashdle Archive keeps a running log. I check it when I'm traveling and miss a day. Streak recovery is possible if you know what you missed. The archive also shows attribute patterns—useful for predicting when a universe is due to return.

sportle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The May 26 Sportle solution is WRIST — as in wrist shot, wristband, the thing you sprain catching a line drive wrong. Not a venue, not a position, just a body part that shows up constantly in sports commentary and equipment names. I burned three guesses on ARENA, COURT, and MOUND before I let go of the "place where sport happens" fixation.

Today's Sportle at a glance

WRIST contains no repeating letters. That alone breaks the pattern for anyone who was hunting a doubled vowel or a consonant cluster like SPORT or SSKI. The W and R are both uncommon starters in general Wordle pools, but W opens a surprising number of sports terms: wrest, wrong (as in wrong-footed), wrist, wring.

I opened with GLOVE — decent for baseball coverage, terrible for today. Got a yellow R on guess two from COURT. The real tell was sliding WATCH into guess four and seeing that W light green. From there it was either WRIST or WRIST — no other five-letter sports W_R_S_ combination exists that I could summon at 6:47 AM.

Letter breakdown:

  • W — position 1
  • R — position 2
  • I — position 3
  • S — position 4
  • T — position 5

If you're the type who tracks past Sportle answers, note this is our first body-part term since April's ANKLE. The game runners seem to be cycling through equipment, venue, body part, position — not strictly, but enough to exploit if you're strategic about second guesses.

What to pay attention to

Sportle's dictionary pulls from general sports usage, not just proper nouns. That means WRIST qualifies through compound terms — wrist shot, wristband, wrist guard — even if "wrist" by itself isn't a piece of equipment you buy at Dick's.

Three things that slowed me down today:

Fixating on venue words. ARENA, COURT, FIELD, MOUND, TRACK — I burned guesses here because the pattern felt "location-y." Don't. Sportle includes body parts, actions (SWING, DRIVE), and equipment terms that aren't venues.

Ignoring W starters. W is a dead letter in standard Wordle strategy. In Sportle, it's live. WRIST, WREST, WEDGE, WAGON (as in wagon train in cycling, or the defensive formation). If you get a W early, don't discard it for an more common consonant.

The S-T ending trap. So many sports terms end S-T: FEAST, BOAST (no), BLAST (borderline), ROAST (no). But also CHEST, TRUST, FIRST. I spent guess five convinced the answer was CHEST because of chest protector. The T at position 5 narrowed it fast once I let the W in.

My revised Sportle opener after 500+ games: something that hits R, S, T, and a vowel spread. CRISP isn't bad. TRASH covers bases. But I'm drifting toward WATCH as a deliberate second guess when first guess returns nothing — W, A, T, C, H covers wrist, watch, catch, hatch (no), and warms up the H for THROW or SHOOT later.

Mistakes that cost guesses

Chasing ball-specific terms when the answer is broader. I saw someone on Twitter (no link, you know how search works) post their grid with BALLS, BASES, MITTS, GLOVE, then give up. WRIST isn't ball-sport exclusive — golfers talk wrist hinge, tennis players snap their wrist on serves, fighters check wrist control. The term's universality is what makes it fair game.

Another costly assumption: repeating letters. After ANKLE and KNEES in recent memory, I default to no-repeat unless the pattern forces it. Today's WRIST rewards that restraint. If you're burning guesses on SWISS or SISSY, you're working against the dictionary.

Time of day bias: European players (Sportle runs on UTC midnight) often note the answers skew American — baseball, football, basketball terms. WRIST is neutral enough to pass, but if you're solving at 00:01 GMT and nothing clicks, consider whether the term might be more common in NFL or MLB broadcast vocabulary than your local sport.

Questions players keep asking

Is WRIST a legitimate sports word, or is Sportle stretching?

It's in. Wrist shot alone justifies it — hockey's fundamental scoring motion. Add wristband (equipment), wrist guard (protective gear), and the injury term "sprained wrist" that ends seasons. The game doesn't require standalone equipment status; it requires sports-context usage. WRIST clears easily.

Why did my guess SCORE show no letters?

Today's answer has no O, E, or C. If SCORE went fully gray, that's useful elimination — but it also means you burned a guess without testing W, R, I, or T. After a blank first guess, pivot to something with W-R-I-S-T spread: WRIST itself isn't playable as a guess if you're solving, but TRASH, WRING, or WRIST (if you cheat) would test multiple slots. Better: use our Sportle solver tool to find valid guesses that fit your revealed pattern.

How often does Sportle use body parts?

Roughly once per month in my tracking — ANKLE, KNEES, WRIST, ELBOW has appeared, SHIN once. They're not clustering them, which makes each one a surprise. The pattern isn't reliable enough to guess blindly, but if you've got _ _ _ S T and can't place it, consider body parts before obscure equipment brands.

What's the best second guess after a blank opener?

Depends on what you played. If your opener was SPORT and got only a yellow T, try something with W, R, I — WRING or WRIST (if testing) or TRICE. The key is moving the T to position 5 if you suspect T-ending, which is common in Sportle. Our Sportle archive shows T-ending answers appear about 18% of the time, higher than standard Wordle's rate.

Does Sportle repeat answers?

Not in my tracking since October 2021. With the sports dictionary estimated at 2,300-2,800 valid answers, they've got runway. WRIST is new to the solution set — I don't see it in any archived grid I can access. If you're playing old games through the archive, you won't hit duplicates yet.

Tomorrow's likely to swing back toward equipment or action terms. I'm keeping EAGLE in my back pocket — golf term, also a score. But that's a guess, not a promise. For today's grid, lock in WRIST and move on.

spotle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Spotle Answer Today – May 26, 2026

Today’s artist is a solo act, not a group, and the genre box came up as the broad category that covers about half the acts in the entire database. That ambiguity is exactly why people burn guesses on band names when they should be narrowing by decade and country first.

The debut year sits in the late-2000s window. If you’re still guessing artists who broke through in the ’90s, you’re working against the hint. Move forward.

What you're looking at today

Spotle drops five locked clues and one open clue per round. Today’s unlocked clues:

  • Genre: Pop (this is a catch-all; don’t overvalue it)
  • Debut year range: 2005–2009
  • Group size: Solo
  • Gender: Female
  • Nationality: Canadian

When I saw the Canadian + solo + female + 2005–2009 stack, my first thought was the obvious one: Carly Rae Jepsen. Wrong debut window—she hit in 2012. Second guess went to Avril Lavigne, but her debut was 2002. That’s the trap. The game uses debut year, not peak popularity year, and a lot of us mentally backdate artists to when we first heard them on the radio.

The correct answer today is Feist. Her debut album Let It Die dropped in 2004, but her breakthrough The Reminder came in 2007. Spotle logs her debut year as 2004, which sits right on the edge of that 2005–2009 range. If your interface rounded or displayed the range differently, that edge case might have cost you a guess. I’ve seen the game do this before—artists with debut years that straddle the boundary get bucketed in ways that feel inconsistent until you check the raw data.

How to read the visual hints

Each clue tile color-shifts after you submit a guess. Here’s what actually matters:

  • Green tile: Exact match. Lock it in mentally and stop guessing that category.
  • Yellow tile: Close but wrong. For debut year, this usually means same decade. For nationality, it sometimes means same continent—though that rule wobbles depending on how the database buckets UK vs. England vs. Britain.
  • Gray tile: No match. If you get gray on gender, you’ve eliminated half the database. That’s high-value information; use it.

Today’s most useful gray was probably genre, if you guessed something like rock or hip-hop early. But since pop is so broad, a yellow there doesn’t narrow much. I usually ignore genre until I have three other clues locked.

One thing that still annoys me: the nationality field. Feist is Canadian, born in Nova Scotia. But the database sometimes conflates Canadian and American for artists who chart heavily in the US. How to read the visual hints

Waffle uses the same tile colors as Wordle, but the strategy flips. In Wordle, you guess full words. Here, you rearrange existing letters. Green means a letter is locked in place. Yellow means it belongs somewhere else in that same word (row or column). White/gray means it's in the other word crossing that position.

Here's how I work it:

  1. Lock every green I can see in the first scan. Usually 2-4 letters.
  2. Build around those anchors. Today's F and A in FLORA were obvious once I saw them.
  3. Use yellows to eliminate impossible positions. If a yellow T is in the middle of a five-letter word, it's not staying there.
  4. White tiles are your swap pool. Don't overcommit early.

The visual hint I always miss: a yellow at an row/column intersection means it could belong in either direction. Our Waffle strategy guide has a full breakdown on intersection reads if you want to stop making my mistake.

Chasing acrosses first. The across words are easier to read left-to-right, so everyone starts there. But Waffle's down words often have fewer valid configurations. I spent a swap trying to make L-I-V-E work somewhere because my brain wanted a familiar word. It wasn't.

COUCH works well for a late-May puzzle because it balances familiarity with just enough structural quirkiness. Meaning and Everyday Use

A couch is an upholstered seat for more than one person, typically found in living rooms or lounges. The word comes from the Old French "coucher," meaning to lie down, which makes sense given its purpose. While some might argue for semantic differences between a couch, a sofa, and a settee, in everyday American English, these terms get swapped constantly. Yes, COUCH is valid in Scrabble and all major word games. It's a standard English noun with no capitalization issues or proper noun complications.

How many times has COUCH appeared as a Wordle answer?

As of May 26, 2026, COUCH has appeared once as the daily Wordle answer. The New York Times generally avoids repeating answers unless it's a special event or anniversary puzzle.

Common five-letter words ending in CH include BEACH, TEACH, CATCH, WATCH, and LUNCH. These are all valid Wordle answers that have appeared or could appear in future puzzles.

Why does COUCH have a silent H?

The silent H in COUCH comes from its French origin. Many English words borrowed from French retain spelling conventions that don't match modern pronunciation, similar to words like APPROACH or RESEARCH.

worldle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The silhouette for May 26, 2026, is Slovakia. I burned two guesses on this one immediately because the northern border curve looks deceptively like a slice of Ukraine if you aren't paying attention to the western jagged edge. The shape is distinctively elongated east-to-west, but that northern dip is the tell. If you guessed a Balkan nation or something further south, the distance percentage likely threw you off, as Central Europe gets crowded fast.

Where in the world is today's answer?

Today's target sits right in the heart of Central Europe, landlocked and sandwiched between Poland to the north, Ukraine to the east, Hungary to the south, and Austria and the Czech Republic to the west. The shape is a bit of a stretched oval with a bite taken out of the top. It's easy to confuse this profile with Hungary, which lies directly south, but Hungary is wider and lacks that specific northern indentation. The key here is recognizing the cluster. When your first guess lands you within 500 kilometers but the direction points sharply north or south, you are likely oscillating within the same regional neighborhood. Check the Worldle archive to see how often these Central European shapes rotate into the daily slot; they appear more frequently than players expect because their distinct borders make for fair but tricky puzzles.

Reading the directional clues

The arrow behavior on this specific date was unforgiving for broad guesses. If you threw out "Europe" as a starter (which wastes a guess, by the way), the arrow pointed northwest. That narrows it down to the continent, sure, but it doesn't help with the specific country. The real data comes from the second and third guesses. I saw players in the comments panicking when a guess in Romania returned a "4%" distance match but an arrow pointing west. That 4% is misleadingly small; it implies proximity, but in Europe, 4% can still mean 300 kilometers. The percentage bar fills up faster in dense regions like the EU than it does for vast countries like Canada or Russia. Use the geography solver tool to cross-reference which countries fall within that shrinking radius. Don't just trust the percentage number; trust the arrow's consistency across three different guesses to triangulate the center point.

Mistakes that waste guesses

The biggest trap today was guessing Russia or Ukraine too early. Because the silhouette has that long eastern tail, eyes glaze over and assume "big eastern country." But the scale is off. Slovakia is compact. Guessing a massive neighbor skews your distance data because the game calculates from the geographic center of the country, not the border closest to your guess. If you guess Ukraine, the center is far to the east, giving you a massive distance error even if your border is technically close. Another common blunder was ignoring the landlocked status. Several top comments showed guesses like Croatia or even Sweden, ignoring the fact that today's shape has no coastline. Always verify if the shape touches water before guessing island nations or coastal states. Save your specific country guesses for when you have confirmed the region. Check the daily hint system if you are unsure about the continent, but try to deduce it from the shape first to keep your streak alive.

Questions players keep asking

Why does the distance percentage change so drastically between guesses?

The percentage represents how much of the maximum possible distance you have covered relative to the game's internal scale, not a literal map measurement. In dense areas like Europe, a 1% change can mean moving 50 kilometers, whereas in South America, 1% might be 200 kilometers. The algorithm normalizes distance based on the size of the target country's bounding box. This is why guessing a neighbor often yields a low percentage like 2-5%, while a country on another continent shows 0%. It is a relative metric, not an absolute one. Focus on the trend: is the number going up? That is all that matters.

How do I distinguish between similar shapes like Hungary and Slovakia?

Look at the northern border. Slovakia's northern border with Poland is jagged and follows the Tatra Mountains, creating a distinct uneven line. Hungary's northern border is smoother and curves differently around Slovakia. Also, check the aspect ratio. Slovakia is wider than it is tall, whereas Hungary is slightly more square-like, though still rectangular. If you are stuck between the two, guess a country to the north of both, like Poland. The arrow will tell you instantly which one you are looking at. If the arrow points south, it is likely Slovakia; if it points southeast, you might be looking at Hungary. For more practice, browse the yesterday's solution to compare silhouettes side-by-side.

Does the game count exclaves or disputed territories in the shape?

Generally, Worldle uses the standard recognized borders for the main contiguous landmass. Small exclaves usually do not appear in the silhouette unless they are significant in size. However, the game's database sometimes lags behind real-world geopolitical shifts or uses a specific dataset that might include or exclude certain border regions. If a shape looks "off" by a tiny sliver, do not let it throw your whole guess. Focus on the main body of the country. The core shape is what the game prioritizes for recognition.

What is the best strategy for landlocked countries?

Start with a large, centrally located country in the suspected continent to get a baseline distance and direction. For Europe, guessing France or Germany is often better than guessing a tiny nation like Luxembourg. Once you have a vector, move perpendicular to that line to triangulate. If you guess Germany and the arrow points East, you know you are looking at Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Austria, or Hungary. Your next guess should be one of those to cut the search space in half. Do not random guess small nations until you have eliminated the large ones that would skew your distance data.
